newsitem.title: USA: CIA, FBI heads to report on new Moscow spy case.
newsitem.headline: CIA, FBI heads to report on new Moscow spy case.

text.p: A CIA officer arrested on charges that he spied for Moscow, will appear in court on Monday, and the heads of the CIA and FBI will hold a joint press conference to report on the arrest, the FBI announced.

John Deutch, the director of central intelligence, and Louis Freeh, director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, will give details of the case at 1 p.m. EST (1800 GMT) at FBI headquarters, FBI spokesman Bill Carter said.
The suspect, a career officer whose identity has not been released, was to appear before a federal magistrate at 11 a.m. (1600 GMT) in Alexandria, Virginia, U.S. officials said.

The CIA and the FBI have been hunting for a second possible Moscow spy inside the CIA since the Feb. 21, 1994, arrest of Aldrich Ames, who is serving a life prison term for selling some of the most sensitive U.S. spy secrets to Moscow over a 10-year period.

The person arrested in the new case appeared to have been spying for Moscow for about two years, a U.S. official said. He said the damage done did not appear to be "anywhere near the magnitude" caused by Ames, who unmasked about three dozen agents and perhaps hundreds of operations.
"Any time you have a spy in your midst, it's bad news," the official said. "The good news is that he was caught, and he was caught quickly."

The New York Times said on Monday that the arrested CIA officer was an instructor who trained other agency personnel. It said he had served overseas and was arrested on Saturday in Virginia after a lengthy investigation.
The suspect reportedly had access to secret material on a wide range of issues involving Russia and the former Soviet Union's Cold War satellite states.
The arrest of Ames, a 31-year career officer, set in motion changes in the U.S. intelligence community that have yet to run their course.

James Woolsey resigned as CIA director in December 1994 after being sharply criticised in Congress for his handling of CIA failings that let Ames spy for Moscow under the CIA's nose for nearly a decade.
